summary: Smooth representations of local groups, Part II: the unitary representation theory of p-adic groups on top of SR.0–SR.6. SRU.0 sets up strongly continuous unitary representations, Hilbert sums, functions of positive type, the GNS construction through Tau Ceti's Kolmogorov space, the unitary dual and pure positive-type functions, and smooth vectors with K-type projectors. SRU.1 develops weak containment, Milman's converse to Krein–Milman, Godement's integrated positive type, weak-* compactness of P≤1, Raikov's theorem, single-coefficient approximation, the Fell topology, the closure theorem for sums and the corrected Gan–Savin Proposition 11.6 and Corollary 11.7 for second-countable locally compact groups. SRU.2 identifies the unitary dual with irreducible unitarizable smooth representations (unitary structures, uniqueness, semisimplicity, unitary induction, completion, Bernstein's admissibility). SRU.3 proves the limit theorems (characters, Miličić, Tadić, K-types, Rodier, Heiermann–Opdam, Gan–Savin 11.2, isolation of discrete series in the tempered dual), and SRU.4 the isolation of the Steinberg representation in rank ≥ 2 and of supercuspidals (finite Steinberg, Barbasch–Moy, Rodier, Howe–Moore). SRU.5–SRU.7 follow Ciubotaru–Harris: real Satake parameters, half-integrality, the generic unitary spherical region and its classification, the half-integral points and the generic temperedness test (stated for real or central-compact parameters), the nonsplit unramified transfer, the Aubert–Zelevinsky involution, Kazhdan–Lusztig parameters and the spherical complementary series with extraneous points. The other Part II directions of SR are proposed as separate roadmaps.

nodes.title: Strongly continuous unitary representations and unitary equivalence
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group and H a complex Hilbert space (NormedAddCommGroup, InnerProductSpace ℂ, CompleteSpace), with Mathlib's inner product ⟪x, y⟫, conjugate-linear in x. A strongly continuous unitary representation of G on H is π : ContRepresentation ℂ G H such that (i) Tau Ceti's ContRepresentation.IsUnitary π holds (⟪π g v, π g w⟫ = ⟪v, w⟫ for all g, v, w), and (ii) π is strongly continuous: for every v ∈ H the orbit map g ↦ π g v is continuous G → H. The predicate (ii) is ContRepresentation.IsStronglyContinuous; it is weaker than continuity of g ↦ π g in the operator norm, the hypothesis of Tau Ceti's ContRepresentation.matrixCoeff. Two such representations (π, H), (ρ, H') are unitarily equivalent, π ≃ᵤ ρ, when there is a linear isometric equivalence T : H ≃ₗᵢ[ℂ] H' with T (π g v) = ρ g (T v) for all g and v. A closed subspace W ⊆ H is invariant when π g W ⊆ W for all g; π is topologically irreducible when H ≠ 0 and the only closed invariant subspaces are 0 and H (the convention of NoncompactQuantumSymmetry M0, distinct from algebraic irreducibility Representation.IsIrreducible).
hypotheses: G a topological group; no local compactness or separation is required for the definitions.
H a complex Hilbert space; inner products are linear in the second variable.
proofSteps: Define IsStronglyContinuous π :⇔ ∀ v, Continuous (fun g ↦ π g v), as a Prop on Mathlib's ContRepresentation, beside Tau Ceti's IsUnitary rather than bundled into a new carrier (OperatorAlgebraDynamics, Scope and conventions, and the open NoncompactQuantumSymmetry roadmap M0 use the same pair of conditions).
Define unitary equivalence through Mathlib's LinearIsometryEquiv and an intertwining equation; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are composition of isometric equivalences.
Norm continuity implies strong continuity because evaluation at v is continuous on V →L[ℂ] V; the converse fails (unit test 3).

For a closed invariant W the restricted action is a ContRepresentation on W (Tau Ceti ContRepresentation.subrepresentation, IsUnitary.subrepresentation), strongly continuous for the subspace topology; the orthogonal complement of an invariant closed subspace is invariant because π g* = π g⁻¹ (Tau Ceti IsUnitary.adjoint_eq_inv).
acceptance: The trivial representation of any G on ℂ is a topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representation.
For a finite-dimensional H, topological irreducibility coincides with Representation.IsIrreducible of π.toRepresentation, since every subspace is closed.

nodes.title: Hilbert direct sums of unitary representations
nodes.statement: For a family (πᵢ, Hᵢ)_{i ∈ ι} of strongly continuous unitary representations of G, the Hilbert direct sum ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ acts coordinatewise on Mathlib's lp (fun i ↦ Hᵢ) 2: (⊕̂ πᵢ)(g) f = (i ↦ πᵢ g (f i)). It is a strongly continuous unitary representation; the coordinate inclusions Hᵢ → lp (fun i ↦ Hᵢ) 2 are isometric intertwiners onto mutually orthogonal closed invariant subspaces whose closed span is the whole space, and the coordinate projections are intertwiners.
hypotheses: ι an arbitrary index type; each πᵢ strongly continuous unitary.
proofSteps: Coordinatewise action preserves the ℓ² norm, so each (⊕̂ πᵢ)(g) is a linear isometry with inverse (⊕̂ πᵢ)(g⁻¹); this gives IsUnitary.

Strong continuity: for f with finite support the orbit map is a finite sum of continuous maps; finitely supported f are dense in lp 2, and an ε/3 argument with the uniform bound ‖(⊕̂ πᵢ)(g)‖ ≤ 1 gives continuity for every f.
The inclusions lp.single i are isometric intertwiners; orthogonality and density of their spans are Mathlib's lp Hilbert-sum facts.
acceptance: The positive-type coefficient of a finitely supported vector f = Σᵢ fᵢ is the sum of the coefficients of the fᵢ (positive-type-coefficient).

sources.match: Gan–Savin form π = ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ from a sequence of irreducible unitary representations and approximate its coefficients through those of the summands.

nodes.title: Functions of positive type on a group
nodes.statement: Let G be a group. A function φ : G → ℂ is of positive type, IsPositiveType φ, when for every n, every c : Fin n → ℂ and every g : Fin n → G, 0 ≤ Σᵢ Σⱼ cᵢ · conj(cⱼ) · φ(gⱼ⁻¹ gᵢ) in the order of ℂ (real and nonnegative); equivalently the kernel (a, b) ↦ φ(a⁻¹ b) is Matrix.PosSemidef. For a topological group, P(G) is the set of continuous φ of positive type ([BHV] Definition C.4.1 requires continuity), P₁(G) = {φ ∈ P(G) : φ(e) = 1} and P≤1(G) = {φ ∈ P(G) : φ(e) ≤ 1}. Basic properties: φ(e) is real and ≥ 0, φ(g⁻¹) = conj φ(g), |φ(g)| ≤ φ(e), and |φ(g) − φ(h)|² ≤ 2 φ(e) (φ(e) − Re φ(g⁻¹h)), so every φ ∈ P(G) is left and right uniformly continuous. P(G) is a convex cone closed under pointwise products, complex conjugation and pointwise limits (continuity of the limit to be checked separately); P₁(G) and P≤1(G) are convex. On G = Multiplicative A for an additive commutative group A, IsPositiveType agrees with Tau Ceti's IsPositiveDefiniteSub.
hypotheses: G a group; continuity is part of membership in P(G), not of IsPositiveType.
The order on ℂ is Mathlib's ComplexOrder: 0 ≤ z iff z is real and nonnegative.
proofSteps: (i)–(ii) are the 1 × 1 and 2 × 2 cases of the defining inequality ([BHV] Proposition C.4.2(i)–(ii), via C.1.2).
(iii) is the 3 × 3 case with the points g, h, e and the scalars chosen in [BHV] Proposition C.4.2(iii).

The kernel form: Σ cᵢ conj(cⱼ) φ(gⱼ⁻¹gᵢ) is the hermitian form of the matrix (φ(gⱼ⁻¹gᵢ)), so IsPositiveType φ iff (fun a b ↦ φ (a⁻¹ * b)) is Matrix.PosSemidef; this is the input to Tau Ceti's Kolmogorov space.
Closure under products is the Schur product theorem for positive semidefinite matrices; under limits, nonnegativity is a closed condition.
For G = Multiplicative A, gⱼ⁻¹ gᵢ = ofAdd (vᵢ − vⱼ), which is the expression in IsPositiveDefiniteSub.
acceptance: Every unitary character χ : G → S¹ is of positive type, and χ ∈ P₁(G) when χ is continuous.
The constant function 1 is an extreme point of P₁(G), being the coefficient of the trivial representation, which is irreducible (pure-iff-irreducible).

sources.locator: Definition C.4.1 and Proposition C.4.2, p. 373
sources.match: Functions of positive type are continuous functions whose kernel (g₁, g₂) ↦ φ(g₂⁻¹g₁) is of positive type; they satisfy φ(g⁻¹) = conj φ(g), |φ(g)| ≤ φ(e) and the uniform-continuity estimate.

sources.locator: §C.5, opening definitions, p. 379 (P(G), P₁(G)); before Lemma C.5.4, p. 382 (P≤1(G))
sources.match: P(G) is the convex cone of functions of positive type and P₁(G) its normalised part; P≤1(G), the φ with ‖φ‖_∞ = φ(e) ≤ 1, is introduced before Lemma C.5.4.
Gan–Savin use the weak-* closed convex hull of normalised positive-type coefficients inside the unit ball of L^∞(G).

nodes.title: Positive-type coefficients of unitary representations
nodes.statement: For a strongly continuous representation π of a topological group G on a complex Hilbert space H and v, w ∈ H, the coefficient coeff π w v ∈ C(G, ℂ) is g ↦ ⟪w, π g v⟫; the positive-type coefficient of v is ptCoeff π v := coeff π v v, g ↦ ⟪v, π g v⟫ (Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette's ⟨π(g)v, v⟩). If π is unitary, ptCoeff π v is of positive type and lies in P(G), with ptCoeff π v (e) = ‖v‖²; ptCoeff π v ∈ P₁(G) for unit vectors v. It is invariant under unitary equivalence, additive on orthogonal sums of invariant subspaces, and ‖ptCoeff π v − ptCoeff π w‖_∞ ≤ (‖v‖ + ‖w‖)‖v − w‖. When g ↦ π g is norm continuous, ptCoeff π v g = Tau Ceti's matrixCoeff π hπ v v (g⁻¹) = conj (matrixCoeff π hπ v v g).
hypotheses: π strongly continuous (for continuity of coefficients); unitary for positive type.
proofSteps: Continuity: g ↦ π g v is continuous and ⟪w, ·⟫ is continuous.
Positive type: Σᵢⱼ cᵢ conj(cⱼ) ⟪v, π(gⱼ⁻¹gᵢ) v⟫ = Σᵢⱼ cᵢ conj(cⱼ) ⟪π gⱼ v, π gᵢ v⟫ = ‖Σᵢ cᵢ π gᵢ v‖² ≥ 0 ([BHV] Proposition C.4.3).
The uniform estimate: |⟪v, π g v⟫ − ⟪w, π g w⟫| ≤ |⟪v − w, π g v⟫| + |⟪w, π g (v − w)⟫| by Cauchy–Schwarz and unitarity.
Comparison with Tau Ceti: matrixCoeff π hπ v v g = ⟪π g v, v⟫ = conj ⟪v, π g v⟫, and ⟪π g⁻¹ v, v⟫ = ⟪v, π g v⟫ by unitarity.
acceptance: For the trivial representation on ℂ, ptCoeff π v is the constant |v|².
For a unit vector v of a one-dimensional representation given by a unitary character χ, ptCoeff π v = χ.

sources.match: Diagonal matrix coefficients g ↦ ⟨π(g)ξ, ξ⟩ of unitary representations are of positive type; they are called the functions of positive type associated to π.

nodes.title: The GNS construction for functions of positive type
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group and φ ∈ P(G). There is a triple (π_φ, H_φ, ξ_φ) with H_φ a complex Hilbert space, π_φ a strongly continuous unitary representation of G on H_φ and ξ_φ ∈ H_φ a cyclic vector (its orbit spans a dense subspace) such that φ = ptCoeff π_φ ξ_φ. It is unique: for any triple (π, H, ξ) with ξ cyclic and ptCoeff π ξ = φ there is a unique unitary equivalence T : π_φ ≃ᵤ π with T ξ_φ = ξ. Concretely H_φ is Tau Ceti's Kolmogorov space of the positive semidefinite kernel K(a, b) = φ(a⁻¹ b), with feature map Φ : G → H_φ satisfying ⟪Φ a, Φ b⟫ = φ(a⁻¹b); π_φ(g) Φ(a) = Φ(g a) and ξ_φ = Φ(e). For any strongly continuous unitary π and v ∈ H, the GNS representation of ptCoeff π v is unitarily equivalent to the cyclic subrepresentation on the closed span of π(G)v. If φ = φ₁ + φ₂ with φ₁, φ₂ ∈ P(G), then π_{φ₁} is unitarily equivalent to a subrepresentation of π_φ ([BHV] Proposition C.5.1).
hypotheses: φ continuous and of positive type.
proofSteps: By positive-type-function the kernel K(a, b) = φ(a⁻¹b) is Matrix.PosSemidef; take H_φ = Matrix.PosSemidef.KolmogorovSpace and Φ = kolmogorovFeature, so ⟪Φ a, Φ b⟫ = K a b and the span of Φ(G) is dense (inner_kolmogorovFeature, kolmogorovFeature_dense).

For g ∈ G the map a ↦ Φ(g a) has the same kernel, since (g a)⁻¹(g b) = a⁻¹b, and dense span; Tau Ceti's kolmogorovEquiv gives a linear isometric equivalence π_φ(g) with π_φ(g)Φ(a) = Φ(ga). Uniqueness of kolmogorovEquiv gives π_φ(gh) = π_φ(g)π_φ(h).

Strong continuity: ‖Φ(ga) − Φ(a)‖² = 2 Re(φ(e) − φ(a⁻¹ g a)), which tends to 0 as g → e by continuity of φ; density and the uniform bound ‖π_φ(g)‖ ≤ 1 extend continuity to all vectors ([BHV] Theorem C.4.10, proof).
ptCoeff π_φ ξ_φ (g) = ⟪Φ e, Φ g⟫ = φ(g).
Uniqueness: for (π, H, ξ) the map Φ(a) ↦ π(a)ξ has the same kernel; kolmogorovIsometry and cyclicity give T, and uniqueness of the extension gives intertwining.

For Proposition C.5.1, domination gives a contraction T : H_φ → H_{φ₁} with dense range, intertwining the actions. T* is injective but need not be isometric. Apply the rectangular polar decomposition to T*: its initial space is all H_{φ₁}, and its polar isometry intertwines, since TT* on H_{φ₁} and its square root commute with the action. This gives the required isometric intertwiner (BHV Proposition A.1.4, pp. 307–308; upstream OperatorTheory/PolarDecomposition PD-B24–B34).
acceptance: For φ = 1, H_φ is one-dimensional and π_φ is trivial.
For G discrete and φ = δ_e, π_φ is the left regular representation on ℓ²(G) ([BHV] Example C.4.12).

sources.locator: Theorem C.4.10 and Definition C.4.11, pp. 376–377
sources.match: Every function of positive type is the coefficient of a cyclic vector in a unitary representation, unique up to an equivalence carrying cyclic vector to cyclic vector; the proof realises the space by the positive kernel and lets G act by left translation.
If φ = φ₁ + φ₂ in P(G) then π_{φ₁} is contained in π_φ, and if π_φ is irreducible then φ₁ is a multiple of φ.
A bounded intertwiner induces a unitary equivalence between the orthogonal complement of its kernel and the closure of its image, via its polar decomposition.
The complete-space rectangular polar factor gives an isometry from the orthogonal complement of the kernel onto the closure of the image; uniqueness yields equivariance for a bounded intertwiner.

nodes.title: The unitary dual
nodes.statement: For a topological group G, the unitary dual Ĝ is the set of unitary-equivalence classes of topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations of G. To avoid quantifying over Hilbert spaces in all universes, Ĝ is realised as the quotient of the set of φ ∈ P₁(G) whose GNS representation π_φ is topologically irreducible by the relation φ ∼ ψ :⇔ π_φ ≃ᵤ π_ψ. For a topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary (π, H) and a unit vector v, [π] := the class of ptCoeff π v, which does not depend on v; [π] = [ρ] iff π ≃ᵤ ρ; every class is [π_φ] for any representative φ.
hypotheses: G a topological group; for the Fell topology and the theorems of SRU.1 G is locally profinite.
proofSteps: Independence of v: in a topologically irreducible π every nonzero v is cyclic (strongly-continuous-unitary, IsTopologicallyIrreducible.cyclic), so by uniqueness in the GNS construction π_{ptCoeff π v} ≃ᵤ π for every unit v.
Hence [π] = [ρ] iff π_{ptCoeff π v} ≃ᵤ π_{ptCoeff ρ w} iff π ≃ᵤ ρ.
Every class is realised by its GNS representation, which is topologically irreducible by definition of the set.
acceptance: For G abelian the unitary dual is in bijection with the continuous unitary characters, every topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representation being one-dimensional (Schur's lemma).
For G compact the classes are those of finite-dimensional irreducibles, matching the index set of Peter–Weyl in RepresentationTheory/CompactGroups.

sources.locator: §F.2, opening paragraph, p. 427; Remark C.4.13, p. 378
sources.match: The family of all unitary representations is not a set; one restricts to sets of equivalence classes, for instance the unitary dual of irreducible ones, or classes of cyclic representations, which are parametrised by a subset of the functions of positive type.
Gan–Savin study the topology of the unitary dual of a split p-adic group and its isolated points.

tests.statement: For a topologically irreducible π and unit vectors v ≠ w, UnitaryDual.mk π v = UnitaryDual.mk π w.

nodes.title: Pure functions of positive type and irreducibility
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group. (1) For φ ∈ P₁(G), φ is an extreme point of P₁(G) iff its GNS representation π_φ is topologically irreducible ([BHV] Theorem C.5.2). (2) The extreme points of P≤1(G) are 0 and the extreme points of P₁(G) ([BHV] Theorem C.5.5(i)). (3) If π is topologically irreducible, strongly continuous and unitary, every normalised coefficient ptCoeff π v, ‖v‖ = 1, is an extreme point of P₁(G) and of P≤1(G). Extreme points are taken in Mathlib's sense, Set.extremePoints ℝ.
hypotheses: G a topological group; φ continuous of positive type with φ(e) = 1 in (1).
proofSteps: If H_φ = W ⊕ Wᗮ is a nontrivial invariant orthogonal decomposition, cyclicity makes both projected cyclic vectors nonzero. Their normalised coefficients give φ = sφ₁+(1−s)φ₂ with 0<s<1. If φ₁=φ, equality of coefficients gives ⟪π(g)ξ,P_Wξ⟫=s⟪π(g)ξ,ξ⟫ for every g. The orbit spans densely, hence P_Wξ=sξ, which is impossible for a projection and a nonzero ξ with 0<s<1. Thus the decomposition is nonconstant (BHV Theorem C.5.2, pp. 380–381). Orthogonal invariant subspaces can carry equivalent representations; disjointness is not used.

If π_φ is irreducible and φ = t φ₁ + (1 − t) φ₂, then t φ₁ ≤ φ in the cone order, so by [BHV] Proposition C.5.1 (gns-construction, gns_add_le) there is a positive operator A in the commutant of π_φ with t φ₁ = ⟪ξ_φ, π_φ(·) A ξ_φ⟫; Schur's lemma for topologically irreducible unitary representations ([BHV] Theorem A.2.2; owned by the open NoncompactQuantumSymmetry roadmap, M0 item 1, see upstreamImports) makes A scalar, so φ₁ = φ.

(2): 0 is extreme in P≤1 because φ(e) = 0 forces φ = 0; an element ψ with 0 < ψ(e) < 1 is the convex combination ψ(e)(ψ/ψ(e)) + (1 − ψ(e))0; normalisation forces both summands of a decomposition of an element of ext P₁ into P₁ ([BHV] Theorem C.5.5(i), proof).
(3) follows from (1)–(2) and the GNS uniqueness: π_{ptCoeff π v} ≃ᵤ π.
acceptance: For G = ℤ/2, P₁(G) is the segment of functions with φ(0) = 1, φ(1) ∈ [−1, 1]; its extreme points φ(1) = ±1 are the two characters, and the midpoint φ(1) = 0, the coefficient of the regular representation, is not extreme.
For G compact the characters of finite-dimensional irreducibles normalised by dimension are not extreme in general, but normalised diagonal coefficients of irreducibles are.

sources.locator: Theorem C.5.2 and its proof, pp. 380–381
sources.match: A normalised function of positive type is extremal iff its GNS representation is irreducible; the proof splits the cyclic vector along an invariant decomposition and uses Proposition C.5.1 with Schur's lemma.
The extreme points of P≤1(G) are those of P₁(G) together with 0.
Gan–Savin invoke [BHV, Theorem C.5.2] for the extremality of normalised coefficients of the irreducible σ and of the πₙ.

nodes.title: Smooth vectors and K-type projectors of unitary representations of locally profinite groups
nodes.statement: Let G be locally profinite (compact open subgroups form a neighbourhood basis of e) and π a strongly continuous unitary representation on H. For a compact open subgroup K: H^K is a closed subspace and e_K is the orthogonal projection onto it; for every open normal K' ⊆ K, e_K = [K : K']⁻¹ Σ_{k ∈ K/K'} π(k) e_{K'}, and e_K v is the average of k ↦ π(k)v for the Haar probability measure of K. The smooth vectors H^∞ = ⋃_K H^K form a dense G-stable subspace; with the restricted action they are a smooth representation in the sense of SR.0 with (H^∞)^K = H^K, on which e_K is SR.0's averaging projector. For a smooth irreducible representation τ of K, trivial on an open normal K' ⊆ K, the K-type projector e_τ := (dim τ / [K : K']) Σ_{k ∈ K/K'} conj(χ_τ(k)) π(k) e_{K'} is the orthogonal projection onto the τ-isotypic subspace H(τ); the H(τ) are mutually orthogonal and H is their Hilbert sum. Equivalently e_τ = π(f_τ) for the smooth function f_τ on G supported on K with f_τ = (dim τ / vol K) conj χ_τ on K; Gan–Savin's normalisation omits the factor dim τ (sourceIssues E1).
hypotheses: G locally profinite; π strongly continuous unitary.
τ a smooth irreducible complex representation of the compact open K (finite-dimensional, trivial on some open normal K').
proofSteps: H^K = ⋂_{k∈K} ker(π(k) − 1) is closed; e_K is Mathlib's orthogonal projection onto it.

For K' ⊆ K open normal, P := [K:K']⁻¹ Σ_{k∈K/K'} π(k) e_{K'} is well defined (e_{K'} is K'-invariant on both sides), self-adjoint, idempotent, with range H^K; hence P = e_K. This is the finite-group averaging that SR.0's averaging-projector uses on smooth vectors.
Density of H^∞: for v ∈ H and ε > 0, strong continuity gives a compact open K with ‖π(k)v − v‖ < ε on K, hence ‖e_K v − v‖ ≤ ε; G-stability: π(g)H^K = H^{gKg⁻¹}.
Smoothness of H^∞: every vector is fixed by a compact open subgroup, so the stabilisers are open (SR.0 is-smooth).

K-type projectors: on H^{K'} the finite group K/K' acts unitarily and e_τ is the classical isotypic projector of a finite group (Schur orthogonality for the finite group K/K'); the H(τ) are orthogonal and their sum contains the dense H^∞. The general compact-group version (vector-valued Haar averaging for any compact K) is the projector P_τ of NoncompactQuantumSymmetry M0; this node is its profinite specialisation by finite sums.
acceptance: For the trivial representation, e_K = 1 and e_τ = 0 for every nontrivial τ.
For π irreducible admissible unitarizable of a reductive p-adic group (SRU.2), H^K is finite-dimensional and e_K H is the completion-independent space V^K.

sources.locator: §2.1, definition of P_K and the sentence after it, p. 20
sources.match: For a smooth representation the projection P_K onto the K-invariants is the normalised integral over K, essentially a finite sum, and V decomposes as V^K ⊕ V(K) as representations of K.
Gan–Savin attach to a K-type τ a smooth function f_τ supported on K with π(f_τ) the projector onto the τ-isotypic subspace of every unitary representation, and use it in Lemma 11.4.
The smooth vectors of a continuous unitary representation of a p-adic group form a dense subspace.

The open roadmap defines P_τ = d_τ ∫_K conj(χ_τ(k)) π(k) dk by vector-valued integration for compact K, with self-adjointness, idempotence and orthogonality; this node is the profinite case by finite sums.

uses.how: the K-type τ of π is detected by ⟨π(f_τ)v, v⟩ ≠ 0, which passes to the approximating coefficients
v and the vₙ may be taken K-fixed, so the coefficients are K-bi-invariant
the smooth vectors of the completion of an admissible unitarizable representation are the representation itself

nodes.title: Weak containment of unitary representations
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group and σ, π strongly continuous unitary representations on Hσ, Hπ. σ is weakly contained in π, σ ≺ π, when for every v ∈ Hσ, every compact Q ⊆ G and every ε > 0 there are w₁, …, wₙ ∈ Hπ with |ptCoeff σ v g − Σᵢ ptCoeff π wᵢ g| < ε for all g ∈ Q ([BHV] Definition F.1.1). Equivalently (normalised convex form, Gan–Savin Definition 11.5, [BHV] Remark F.1.2): every normalised coefficient ptCoeff σ v, ‖v‖ = 1, is a uniform limit on compact sets of convex combinations of normalised coefficients ptCoeff π w, ‖w‖ = 1. σ and π are weakly equivalent, σ ∼ π, if σ ≺ π and π ≺ σ. It suffices to test v in a subset whose G-translates span a dense subspace ([BHV] Lemma F.1.3).
hypotheses: G a topological group; all representations strongly continuous and unitary.
proofSteps: Equivalence of the two forms: if a sum Σ ψᵢ of coefficients of π approximates a normalised φ uniformly on a compact Q ∋ e, then Σ ψᵢ(e) is close to 1 and Σ (ψᵢ(e)/Σⱼψⱼ(e)) (ψᵢ/ψᵢ(e)) is a convex combination of normalised coefficients close to φ on Q; the converse rescales ([BHV] Remark F.1.2).
Reflexivity and invariance under unitary equivalence are immediate; transitivity substitutes approximations, using that coefficients of π are uniformly continuous in the vector (dist_ptCoeff_le).

A closed invariant subrepresentation or a Hilbert summand of π is weakly contained in π; a Hilbert sum ⊕̂ σᵢ ≺ π iff every σᵢ ≺ π, because the coefficient of a finitely supported vector is the sum of the coefficients of its components and finitely supported vectors are dense.

For Lemma F.1.3, first fix one test vector: expand coefficients of its finite linear combinations of translates, on the enlarged compact sets gᵢ⁻¹Qgⱼ. For different test vectors use the argument of BHV pp. 421–423: the vectors with approximable coefficients form a closed G-invariant subspace; to prove closure under addition, project one cyclic subspace into the orthogonal complement of the other and use Proposition A.1.4 to identify the resulting cyclic representation with a subrepresentation of the second. Orthogonal sums then give coefficient sums. Expanding cross terms for two unrelated test vectors does not suffice.
acceptance: σ ≺ σ ⊕̂ ρ for every ρ.
For G compact and σ irreducible, σ ≺ π iff σ is unitarily equivalent to a subrepresentation of π ([BHV] Proposition F.1.8).

sources.locator: Definition F.1.1, Remark F.1.2, Lemma F.1.3, pp. 420–422
sources.match: π ≺ ρ when every function of positive type associated to π is a uniform limit on compacta of sums of functions associated to ρ; for normalised functions one may use convex combinations of normalised ones; it suffices to check on a set of vectors with total translates.
σ is weakly contained in π when each normalised coefficient of σ is approximated uniformly on compact sets by convex combinations of normalised coefficients of π.

sources.locator: Appendix F.1, Lemma F.1.3 and proof, pp. 421–423; Appendix A.1, Proposition A.1.4, pp. 307–308
sources.match: Testing on a set whose translates span densely is sufficient; the proof handles sums of cyclic subspaces using an equivariant polar decomposition.
The complete-space rectangular polar factor gives an isometry from the orthogonal complement of the kernel onto the closure of the image; uniqueness yields equivariance for a bounded intertwiner.

uses.how: the L² spaces of local homogeneous spaces are weakly contained in automorphic L² spaces, via Poincaré series
the hypothesis σ ≺ ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ
convergence of nets in the Fell topology is weak containment in the sums over subnets

api.statement: For a family (πᵢ): σ ≺ ⊕̂ πᵢ :⇔ ∀ v, ∀ Q compact, ∀ ε > 0, ∃ finitely many (i_j, w_j), ∀ g ∈ Q, ‖ptCoeff σ v g − Σ_j ptCoeff π_{i_j} w_j g‖ < ε; σ ≺ π is the case of a one-member family.

api.statement: σ ≺ π iff each normalised ptCoeff σ v lies in the closure, for uniform convergence on compacta, of the convex hull of the normalised coefficients of π.

api.name: WeaklyContained.refl
api.statement: σ ≺ σ.

api.name: WeaklyContained.trans

api.name: WeaklyContained.of_unitaryEquiv

api.name: WeaklyContained.of_subrepresentation
api.statement: A closed invariant subrepresentation of π is weakly contained in π.

api.name: hilbertSum_weaklyContained_iff
api.statement: hilbertSum σ ≺ π ↔ ∀ i, σ i ≺ π.

api.statement: If the coefficients of vectors in a set S ⊆ Hσ with dense span of G-translates are approximable, then σ ≺ π ([BHV] Lemma F.1.3).

tests.statement: Every strongly continuous unitary representation is weakly contained in itself.

tests.name: trivial_weaklyContained_regular_int
tests.statement: For G = ℤ (discrete), the trivial representation is weakly contained in the left regular representation on ℓ²(ℤ): the unit vectors (2N+1)^{-1/2} 1_{[−N, N]} have coefficients tending to 1 uniformly on finite sets.

tests.statement: For G = ℤ the left regular representation on ℓ²(ℤ) has no nonzero invariant vector, so weak containment of the trivial representation is not containment.

tests.name: weaklyContained_finite_iff
tests.statement: For G finite and σ irreducible, σ ≺ π iff Hom_G(σ, π) ≠ 0.

nodes.title: Milman's converse to the Krein–Milman theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be a real Hausdorff topological vector space that is locally convex (Mathlib's LocallyConvexSpace ℝ E), F ⊆ E, and suppose C := closure (convexHull ℝ F) is compact. Then every extreme point of C lies in closure F: Set.extremePoints ℝ C ⊆ closure F. Mathlib's closure_convexHull_extremePoints is the Krein–Milman theorem (C is the closed convex hull of its extreme points); this is its converse.
hypotheses: E real, Hausdorff, locally convex; complex spaces are used through restriction of scalars.
closure (convexHull ℝ F) compact.
proofSteps: Let x ∈ ext C and suppose x ∉ closure F. Since closure F ⊆ C is compact, choose a closed convex neighbourhood U of 0 with x ∉ closure F + U + U (local convexity and regularity of the uniform structure).
Cover closure F by finitely many translates yᵢ + U, yᵢ ∈ closure F, and put Cᵢ := closure (convexHull (closure F ∩ (yᵢ + U))) ⊆ yᵢ + U, a compact convex set.
The convex hull of the finite union of compact convex Cᵢ is the image of a simplex times ∏ Cᵢ, hence compact; it contains F, so it equals C.
Write x = Σ tᵢ cᵢ with cᵢ ∈ Cᵢ; extremality of x in C forces x = cᵢ for some i (Mathlib's extremePoints_convexHull_subset in the finite form), so x ∈ yᵢ + U ⊆ closure F + U, a contradiction.
acceptance: In ℝ with F = {0, 1} ∪ {1/2}, C = [0, 1] and its extreme points 0, 1 lie in F.
In ℝ² with F the circle, C is the closed disc and its extreme points are exactly the circle = closure F.

Compactness cannot be dropped: in ℓ²(ℕ) with the norm topology and F the standard basis {eₙ}, the closed convex hull C contains 0 (as the limit of (e₁ + ⋯ + eₙ)/n), 0 is extreme in C because C lies in the positive cone, and 0 ∉ closure F since every ‖eₙ‖ = 1; C is not compact.

sources.match: Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette use the standard fact that an extreme point of a compact convex set C, the closed convex hull of F, lies in the closure of F, citing Conway's Theorem 7.8.
Gan–Savin conclude that an extremal point of the weak-* closed convex hull C of F lies in the closure of F, attributing it to the Krein–Milman theorem in Conway's book.

sources.locator: J. B. Conway, A course in functional analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem V.7.8 (not read)
sources.match: The cited textbook statement of Milman's converse.

nodes.title: Positive type through the integrated form
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. Every φ ∈ P(G) is bounded and continuous, so it defines an element of L^∞(G, μ) with ‖φ‖_∞ = φ(e). Conversely, φ ∈ L^∞(G, μ) agrees μ-almost everywhere with a continuous function of positive type iff ∫∫ f(x) conj(f(y)) φ(y⁻¹x) dμ(x) dμ(y) ≥ 0 for every f ∈ C_c(G), equivalently ⟨φ, f* ∗ f⟩ ≥ 0 for every f ∈ L¹(G) ([BHV] Lemma C.5.3, after Godement).
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
proofSteps: φ ∈ P(G) is bounded by φ(e) (positive-type-function) and continuous; ‖φ‖_∞ = φ(e) because φ is continuous at e.
The integrated inequality for continuous φ is the limit of the finite sums defining positive type (Riemann-sum approximation of the double integral on the compact support of f).

The converse is Godement’s representation theorem for a positive bounded functional on the convolution algebra L¹(G): construct its nondegenerate integrated GNS representation and recover its continuous positive-type coefficient. Comparing the L¹ pairings identifies that coefficient with φ almost everywhere. BHV Lemma C.5.3, p. 382, states this result and refers to Folland (3.35) and Dixmier 13.4.4; it does not supply the proof. The integrated-GNS comparison is an explicit gap below. An arbitrary approximate-identity family has not been proved uniformly equicontinuous, so continuity cannot be inferred that way.
acceptance: For G discrete, the integrated condition with f = Σ cᵢ δ_{gᵢ} is literally the defining finite sum.
The constant function −1 fails the integrated test for any f ≠ 0 with ∫ f ≠ 0.

sources.match: A function in L^∞(G) agrees locally almost everywhere with a continuous function of positive type iff ⟨φ, f* ∗ f⟩ ≥ 0 for all f ∈ L¹(G); the proof is in Folland and Dixmier.

sources.locator: G. B. Folland, A course in abstract harmonic analysis, (3.35); J. Dixmier, Les C*-algèbres et leurs représentations, 13.4.4 (not read)
sources.match: The cited proofs.

nodes.title: Weak-* compactness of P≤1(G)
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. With L^∞(G, μ) identified with the dual of L¹(G, μ) through the integral pairing (BanachSpaceTheory B5), the set P≤1(G) is weak-* compact and convex; its extreme points are 0 and the pure functions of positive type (SRU.0 pure-iff-irreducible); the convex hull of ext P₁(G) is weak-* dense in P₁(G) ([BHV] Lemma C.5.4 and Theorem C.5.5).
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
proofSteps: P≤1(G) lies in the closed unit ball of L^∞(G) = L¹(G)* (positive-type-integral-form: ‖φ‖_∞ = φ(e) ≤ 1), which is weak-* compact (Mathlib's WeakDual.isCompact_closedBall, Banach–Alaoglu).
P≤1(G) is weak-* closed: the integrated inequalities ⟨φ, f* ∗ f⟩ ≥ 0 are closed conditions, and positive-type-integral-form returns a continuous function of positive type; φ(e) ≤ 1 is ‖φ‖_∞ ≤ 1.

Krein–Milman (Mathlib's closure_convexHull_extremePoints) gives density of the convex hull of ext P≤1(G) = ext P₁(G) ∪ {0} in P≤1(G); renormalising an approximating net as in [BHV] Theorem C.5.5(ii) gives density in P₁(G).
acceptance: For G discrete, P₁(G) is itself weak-* compact, since φ(e) = ⟨φ, δ_e⟩ is weak-* continuous ([BHV] after Lemma C.5.4).
For G = S¹, compact but not discrete, the characters χₙ ∈ P₁ tend weak-* to 0 ∉ P₁ (Riemann–Lebesgue), so P₁(G) is not weak-* closed ([BHV] Remark C.5.7); compactness holds for P≤1(G) only.

sources.locator: Lemma C.5.4 and Theorem C.5.5, pp. 382–383
sources.match: P≤1(G) is weak-* compact in L^∞(G); its extreme points are those of P₁(G) and 0; the convex hull of ext P₁(G) is weak-* dense in P₁(G).
L^∞(G) is the dual of L¹(G), its unit ball is weak-* compact by Alaoglu's theorem, and the weak-* closed convex hull of normalised coefficients is compact.

nodes.title: Raikov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. On P₁(G) the weak-* topology (from L^∞ = (L¹)*) and the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of G coincide ([BHV] Theorem C.5.6). Consequently the convex hull of the pure normalised functions of positive type is dense in P₁(G) for uniform convergence on compacta (Proposition C.5.8).
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
proofSteps: Uniform on compacta ⇒ weak-*: for f ∈ L¹ and ε > 0 choose a compact Q carrying all but ε of ∫|f|; on Q the functions are uniformly close, off Q they are bounded by 1 ([BHV] proof of C.5.6, first part).

Weak-* ⇒ uniform on compacta: for a net φᵢ → φ in P₁(G) weak-*, choose f ∈ C_c(G) with f ≥ 0, ∫ f = 1 supported near e so that φ is close to 1 there; the convolutions f ∗ φᵢ converge to f ∗ φ uniformly on compacta (equicontinuity of translates of f in L¹), and the estimate |ψ(x) − (f ∗ ψ)(x)|² ≤ 2 Re(1 − ⟨ψ, f⟩)-type bound from positive-type-function (C.4.2(iii)) controls φᵢ − f ∗ φᵢ uniformly once ⟨φᵢ, f⟩ → ⟨φ, f⟩ is close to 1 ([BHV] proof of C.5.6, second part).
Density: combine with positive-type-weak-star-compact.
acceptance: The statement fails on P≤1(G): for G = S¹ the characters χₙ ∈ P₁ converge weak-* to 0 but χₙ(1) = 1 ([BHV] Remark C.5.7).
For G discrete both topologies are pointwise convergence on P₁(G).

sources.locator: Theorem C.5.6 and proof, Remark C.5.7, Proposition C.5.8, pp. 384–386
sources.match: On P₁(G) the weak-* topology and the topology of uniform convergence on compacta coincide; this fails on P≤1(G); hence the convex hull of the pure functions is dense in P₁(G) for uniform convergence on compacta.
By a theorem of Raikov [BHV, Theorem C.5.6] the weak-* limit is a uniform limit on compacta.

nodes.title: Irreducible weak containment by single coefficients
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. Let σ be topologically irreducible and σ ≺ π. Then for every unit v ∈ Hσ the normalised coefficient ptCoeff σ v is a uniform limit on compact subsets of normalised coefficients ptCoeff π w, ‖w‖ = 1, of π itself, not only of their convex combinations ([BHV] Proposition F.1.4). For a family (πᵢ) and σ ≺ ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ, the approximating coefficients can be chosen each a normalised coefficient of a single πᵢ.
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
σ topologically irreducible; π strongly continuous unitary.
proofSteps: Let F be the set of normalised coefficients of π (for a family, the union over i of those of πᵢ), and C the weak-* closure of its convex hull in L^∞(G) = L¹(G)* (BanachSpaceTheory B5, see upstreamImports); C ⊆ P≤1(G) is compact and convex (positive-type-weak-star-compact).
By weak containment ptCoeff σ v ∈ C (uniform convergence on compacta implies weak-* convergence for bounded functions: raikov, easy half).
ptCoeff σ v is extreme in P≤1(G) (pure-iff-irreducible), hence in C; milman-converse puts it in the weak-* closure of F.
A net in F ⊆ P₁(G) converging weak-* to a point of P₁(G) converges uniformly on compacta (raikov).

For G locally profinite this last step is elementary (Gan–Savin, proof of Proposition 11.6): taking v and the approximants fixed by a small compact open K, the coefficients are K-bi-invariant and uniform convergence on compacta is pointwise convergence on K-double cosets, tested against the normalised indicators of KgK (smooth-vectors-unitary).
acceptance: For G finite, σ irreducible and σ ≺ π, the statement gives a unit vector of π whose coefficient equals ptCoeff σ v exactly, since uniform approximation on the finite set G by a compact set of coefficients attains the limit.

The conclusion fails for reducible σ: for G = ℤ/2, σ the regular representation and π = 1 ⊕ sgn, σ ≺ π but the coefficient of (1, 1)/√2 in σ, the indicator of 0, is not a normalised coefficient of 1 or of sgn.

sources.locator: Proposition F.1.4 and its proof, p. 423
sources.match: If an irreducible π is weakly contained in ρ, each normalised positive-type function of π is approximated uniformly on compacta by normalised positive-type functions associated to ρ; the proof uses compactness of the weak-* closed convex hull, extremality and Raikov's theorem.

For p-adic G one may take v and the vₙ fixed by a small compact open K, so the coefficients are K-bi-invariant and uniform convergence on compacta reduces to pointwise convergence on K-double cosets; Gan–Savin call this step banal.

uses.how: the extremal limit coefficient is approximated by single coefficients of the πₙ
the same argument for metaplectic covers Mp_2n(F_S) and products with compact groups
neighbourhoods of an irreducible point are described by single coefficients ([BHV] Proposition F.2.4)

nodes.title: The Fell topology on the unitary dual
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group and Ĝ its unitary dual (SRU.0). For x = [π] ∈ Ĝ, positive-type coefficients φ₁, …, φₙ of π, a compact Q ⊆ G and ε > 0, let W(x, φ₁, …, φₙ, Q, ε) be the set of y = [ρ] ∈ Ĝ such that each φᵢ is within ε on Q of a finite sum of positive-type coefficients of ρ. These sets form a basis of the Fell topology on Ĝ ([BHV] Definition F.2.1). A net yⱼ converges to x iff π ≺ ⊕̂_{k} ρ_k for the representatives ρ_k of every subnet ([BHV] Proposition F.2.2); for G as in SRU.1 irreducible-weak-containment, single normalised coefficients of ρ suffice in W ([BHV] Proposition F.2.4). For a sequence (xₙ), the limit points L[xₙ] (xₙ → x) and cluster points C[xₙ] (x a limit point of a subsequence) satisfy L ⊆ C; x ∈ L[xₙ] iff for some, equivalently every, unit v there are unit vₙ with ptCoeff πₙ vₙ → ptCoeff π v uniformly on compacta (Gan–Savin §11.1). x is isolated when {x} is open. The support of a unitary representation π is supp π = {x ∈ Ĝ : rep x ≺ π}, a closed subset ([BHV] Definition F.2.6). Ĝ is not Hausdorff in general, so L[xₙ] can have several points.
hypotheses: G a topological group for the definition; G as in SRU.1 irreducible-weak-containment for the single-coefficient basis and the 'some, equivalently every' clause.
The criterion using one sequence of single normalised coefficients assumes G second-countable locally compact; the basic topology and net formulation retain their stated generality.
proofSteps: For intersections of basic neighbourhoods centred at x, combine coefficient lists and compact sets and reduce ε. For the full basis axiom at any point y in such a set, take the finitely many approximating vectors witnessing membership, keep the positive error slack, and approximate their coefficients at a nearby representation. The triangle inequality yields a basic neighbourhood of y contained in the original set (BHV Definition F.2.1, pp. 425–426).

Net characterisation: membership of y in W(x, …) is an approximation of finitely many coefficients of x by sums of coefficients of y; along a net this is weak containment in the Hilbert sum over any subnet ([BHV] Proposition F.2.2).
Single coefficients: by irreducible-weak-containment, if x is approximated by sums of coefficients of a net it is approximated by single normalised coefficients ([BHV] Proposition F.2.4).

For the sequence criterion assume G second countable and locally compact. A nonzero vector in an irreducible representation is cyclic. Approximate any other vector by a finite linear combination of its translates; the same combination of the per-index approximating vectors controls its coefficient on enlarged compact sets. Renormalise and diagonalise over a compact exhaustion with errors tending to zero. This preserves the index n and proves some ⇒ every and convergence. Weak containment in the sum over the entire sequence alone proves only membership in its closure, not convergence.
supp π is closed: if x is in its closure, approximations of coefficients of x by sums of coefficients of points of supp π, themselves approximated by coefficients of π, compose.
acceptance: For G finite (discrete and compact) the Fell topology on Ĝ is discrete ([BHV] Example F.2.5(ii)).

For SL₂ or PGL₂ over a p-adic field, the end of the spherical complementary series converges to both the trivial and the Steinberg representation, so L[xₙ] has two points and Ĝ is not Hausdorff (see SRU.4 steinberg-isolated, rank-one non-example).

sources.locator: Definition F.2.1, Propositions F.2.2 and F.2.4, Example F.2.5, Definition F.2.6, pp. 427–429
sources.match: The Fell topology is generated by the sets W(π, φ₁, …, φₙ, Q, ε); convergence of nets is weak containment in sums over subnets; at irreducible points single coefficients suffice; it is discrete for compact groups, the dual topology for abelian groups, and not Hausdorff for the ax + b group; the support of π is the set of irreducibles weakly contained in π.

Gan–Savin define limit points by uniform convergence on compacta of matrix coefficients for some, equivalently any, coefficient, cluster points as limit points of subsequences, note L ⊆ C, and that the unitary dual is not Hausdorff.

uses.how: Miličić's theorem identifies L[πₙ] = C[πₙ] with the constituents of the character limit
isolation of the Steinberg representation is a statement about the Fell topology
isolation of discrete series in the generic automorphic spectrum with respect to the Fell topology

nodes.title: Weak containment of sums and Fell closure
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. For subsets S, T ⊆ Ĝ, the Hilbert sum ⊕_{x∈S} rep x is weakly contained in ⊕_{y∈T} rep y iff S ⊆ closure T in the Fell topology; in particular the two sums are weakly equivalent iff closure S = closure T ([BHV] Exercise F.6.4). Weak containment ignores multiplicities: ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ ∼ ⊕_{y ∈ T} rep y for T the set of classes of the πᵢ.
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
proofSteps: (⇐) If x ∈ closure T, every basic neighbourhood W(x, φ, Q, ε) meets T, so each coefficient of rep x is approximated by sums of coefficients of a single summand of ⊕_T; hence rep x ≺ ⊕_T, and hilbertSum_weaklyContained_iff gives ⊕_S ≺ ⊕_T.

(⇒) For x ∈ S, rep x ≺ ⊕_T with rep x irreducible; irreducible-weak-containment (family form) approximates each normalised coefficient of rep x by a normalised coefficient of a single rep y, y ∈ T; so every basic neighbourhood of x meets T.

Multiplicities: a coefficient of a finitely supported vector of ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ is a sum of coefficients of the πᵢ, each of which is a coefficient of rep [πᵢ] by unitary equivalence; conversely each rep y, y ∈ T, is a summand.
acceptance: With S = T the statement is reflexivity; with T = ∅ it says only S = ∅ is weakly contained in the zero representation.
For G = ℤ and T the set of characters n ↦ e^{inθ} with θ/2π rational, closure T is the whole circle, so the trivial representation, indeed every character, is weakly contained in ⊕_T.

sources.match: For subsets S, T of the unitary dual, ⊕_{σ∈S} σ is weakly contained in ⊕_{τ∈T} τ iff S lies in the Fell closure of T; the two sums are weakly equivalent iff the closures agree.

The weak-containment hypothesis of Proposition 11.6 is the case S = {σ}, T = {[πᵢ]} of this exercise; the paper's sequential conclusion is replaced by this set-closure statement (PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23-B/E17).

nodes.title: Gan–Savin Proposition 11.6, corrected
nodes.statement: Let G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use. Let (πᵢ)_{i ∈ ι} be topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations, π = ⊕̂ᵢ πᵢ, and σ a topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representation with σ ≺ π. Then [σ] lies in the Fell closure of {[πᵢ] : i ∈ ι}. No convergence of a subsequence with increasing original indices is asserted: for G = G₂(ℚ₅), π₁ = σ = St_G and πₙ = 1_G for n ≥ 2, σ ≺ π while every increasing subsequence is eventually 1_G, which does not converge to the isolated point [St_G] (Proposition 11.3, SRU.4).
hypotheses: G a second-countable locally compact group with a left Haar measure μ. This covers reductive groups over local fields, finite central covers such as Mp_2n(F_S), and finite products of these with compact groups, the generality Gan–Savin (Proposition 10.5) and Gan–Ichino (Proposition A.2) use.
ι arbitrary (Gan–Savin take ι = ℕ).
proofSteps: Apply weak-containment-sum-closure with S = {[σ]} and T = {[πᵢ]}, using that π is weakly equivalent to ⊕_{y ∈ T} rep y.

Gan–Savin's proof (weak-* compactness of the closed convex hull of normalised coefficients in L^∞(G), extremality by [BHV] Theorem C.5.2, the Krein–Milman converse and K-bi-invariance) is the argument of irreducible-weak-containment; it produces approximating coefficients from the set of summands, not along an increasing subsequence (PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23-B/E17).
acceptance: The counterexample to the printed subsequence form: G = G₂(ℚ₅), π₁ = St_G, πₙ = 1_G (n ≥ 2); σ = St_G ≺ π trivially, [St_G] ∈ closure {[πᵢ]} because it is [π₁], and no increasing subsequence converges to [St_G].
If the [πᵢ] are pairwise distinct and [σ] is not among them, the conclusion still produces a net of distinct [πᵢ] converging to [σ].

sources.match: Gan–Savin state that an irreducible unitary σ weakly contained in the Hilbert sum of a sequence of irreducible unitary πₙ is a limit of a subsequence of the πₙ; the correct conclusion is the closure statement (PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23-B/E17).
The set-closure formulation of weak containment of sums.

nodes.title: Isolated representations weakly contained in a sum are summands
nodes.statement: In the setting of gan-savin-closure, if moreover [σ] is isolated in Ĝ, or more generally isolated in a subset R ⊆ Ĝ with the induced Fell topology such that R contains [σ] and every [πᵢ], then σ is unitarily equivalent to πᵢ for some i (Gan–Savin Corollary 11.7; the relative form is the one Gan–Ichino use, with R the generic unitary representations of Mp_2n(F_S) with exponents bounded by c < ½). In particular, for G = G₁ × ⋯ × G_m × C with each Gⱼ a reductive p-adic group and C compact, an irreducible σ = σ₁ ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ σ_m ⊗ σ_C whose p-adic factors are isolated in the unitary duals of the Gⱼ and that is weakly contained in a Hilbert sum of irreducibles is one of the summands.
hypotheses: Setting of gan-savin-closure; [σ] isolated.

For the product statement: isolation of [σ] in Ĝ follows from isolation of each [σⱼ] in Ĝⱼ and discreteness of Ĉ, via the product description of the unitary dual of a product with a compact factor (each irreducible of G × C is an outer tensor product with a finite-dimensional irreducible of C).
proofSteps: {[σ]} is open and meets closure {[πᵢ]} (gan-savin-closure), hence meets {[πᵢ]}: [σ] = [πᵢ] for some i, so σ ≃ᵤ πᵢ (UnitaryDual.mk_eq_mk_iff).
Relative form: {[σ]} is open in R and meets closure {[πᵢ]} ∩ R, the closure of {[πᵢ]} in R, hence meets {[πᵢ]}.

For a compact factor C, its finite-dimensional irreducible τ-isotypic projector (NoncompactQuantumSymmetry M0) gives an open condition near σ⊗τ. Compactness and Schur identify the τ-isotypic part with a Hilbert multiplicity space tensored with τ, and the commuting G-action acts on that space. Test finitely many coefficients on a basis of τ to transfer isolation from G to G×C. For several reductive factors also use the type-I tensor-product and Fell-topology compatibility; this requires the precise product-dual theorem, recorded as a gap below. Discreteness of Ĉ alone does not prove a product homeomorphism.
acceptance: Without isolation the statement fails: the trivial representation of ℤ is weakly contained in the Hilbert sum of the characters n ↦ e^{inθ}, θ ≠ 0 rational multiples of 2π, without being one of them.

sources.match: If σ is irreducible, isolated in the unitary dual and weakly contained in the Hilbert sum of the πᵢ, then σ is isomorphic to some πᵢ.

sources.locator: §10.2, proof of Proposition 10.5, pp. 28–29; §10.3, proof of Proposition 10.7, pp. 29–30
sources.match: In Proposition 10.5 Gan–Savin apply the corollary to a finite product of local groups, the components at real places being finite-dimensional, with supercuspidal and Steinberg components isolated by Proposition 11.3; in Proposition 10.7 they apply Proposition 11.6 together with the isolation hypothesis on the δᵢ.

sources.locator: Corollary 11.7, p. 33, with the corrected Proposition 11.6
sources.match: The corollary survives the correction of Proposition 11.6 because an isolated point of a closure belongs to the set (PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23-B/E17).

sources.locator: Appendix A.1, proof of Proposition A.2, arXiv v3 pp. 31–32
sources.match: Gan–Ichino show π_S is weakly contained in the Hilbert sum of the Π_i, that all Π_{i,S} lie in the set of generic unitary representations of Mp_2n(F_S) with exponents bounded by c < ½, and that π_S is isolated in that set for the Fell topology, which forces π_S = Π_{i,S} for some i.

nodes.title: Unitary structures on smooth representations
nodes.statement: Let G be locally profinite and (ρ, V) a smooth complex representation (SR.0). A unitary structure on V is a positive-definite hermitian form on V (an InnerProductSpace.Core ℂ V, conjugate-linear in the first variable) that is G-invariant: ⟪ρ g v, ρ g w⟫ = ⟪v, w⟫. V is not assumed complete ([Ber92] Definition 27). ρ is unitarizable, Representation.IsUnitarizable ρ, when a unitary structure exists. Subrepresentations and finite direct sums of unitarizable representations are unitarizable; twisting by a unitary smooth character preserves unitarizability; an irreducible unitarizable representation has a unitary central character ([Ber92] Proposition 40); for admissible unitarizable V the form gives a G-isomorphism from V onto the complex conjugate of the smooth dual Ṽ ([Ber92] Ch. IV §1.1, Remark 2; [Cas95] after Proposition 2.1.11).
hypotheses: G locally profinite; V a smooth complex representation; no topology on V is used.
For the central-character and contragredient statements: G countable at infinity (σ-compact), as Schur's lemma SR.0 countable-schur requires, or V admissible.
proofSteps: Define IsUnitarizable ρ :⇔ ∃ c : InnerProductSpace.Core ℂ V, ∀ g v w, c.inner (ρ g v) (ρ g w) = c.inner v w. The form is data on V, not an InnerProductSpace instance, because a given V can carry many (Tau Ceti's CompactGroups README makes the same choice for averaged forms).
Subrepresentations restrict the form; finite direct sums take the orthogonal sum; |χ| = 1 gives invariance of the same form for ρ ⊗ χ.
Central character: for z central and v ≠ 0 in an irreducible V, ρ(z)v = ω(z)v (Schur, SR.0 countable-schur), and invariance gives |ω(z)|² ⟪v, v⟫ = ⟪v, v⟫.
The map v ↦ ⟪v, ·⟫ is a conjugate-linear G-map V → Ṽ (smooth because v is fixed by a compact open subgroup); for admissible V it is onto Ṽ by finite dimensionality of each V^K (SR.0 smooth-dual (3)).
acceptance: Every unitary character χ : G → S¹ with open kernel is unitarizable on ℂ.
For G = F^× and χ = |·|, the smooth character χ is not unitarizable, since its values are not of modulus one.

sources.locator: Ch. IV §1.1, Definition 27 and Remarks 1–2, p. 83; Proposition 40, p. 85
sources.match: A G-module is unitary when it carries a positive definite invariant scalar product, completeness not being assumed; for irreducible unitary modules the complex conjugate is the contragredient; unitary representations have unitary central characters.
A smooth irreducible representation is unitarizable if it has a G-invariant positive-definite hermitian form, equivalently if it is the smooth part of an irreducible unitary representation.

sources.locator: §2.1, Proposition 2.1.5 and the paragraph after Proposition 2.1.11, pp. 20–22
sources.match: For admissible unitary representations the hermitian form identifies V with the contragredient, compatibly with orthogonal complements.

uses.how: unitarizable smooth representations are the objects of the unitary dual in the smooth picture
L(ν) is unitary means the spherical representation is unitarizable
the input of the completion functor

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the unitary structure
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients. If V is an irreducible admissible representation of G (every irreducible is admissible, SR.3a), any two G-invariant positive-definite hermitian forms on V are proportional by a positive real constant ([Ber92] Ch. IV §1.1, Lemma 38; [Cas95] Proposition 2.1.15).
hypotheses: G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients.
V irreducible smooth (hence admissible).
proofSteps: A G-invariant hermitian form is a G-map from V to the conjugate-linear dual, landing in its smooth part, the complex conjugate of Ṽ.
Ṽ is irreducible and admissible for irreducible admissible V (SR.3a admissibility-of-irreducibles), so Hom_G(V, conj Ṽ) is at most one-dimensional by Schur's lemma.
Two positive forms differ by a nonzero scalar, real and positive since both are positive on any nonzero vector.
acceptance: For a reducible unitarizable V = W ⊕ W with W irreducible, the forms ⟪·,·⟫ ⊕ 2⟪·,·⟫ and ⟪·,·⟫ ⊕ ⟪·,·⟫ are not proportional, so irreducibility is needed.

sources.locator: Ch. IV §1.1, Lemma 38 and proof, p. 84
sources.match: For an irreducible module of a reductive group there is at most one invariant scalar product up to a constant: hermitian forms are maps to the anti-linear dual, which is admissible irreducible, and Schur's lemma applies.
An irreducible admissible unitary representation has a unique invariant hermitian inner product up to scalars.

nodes.title: Admissible unitarizable representations are semisimple
nodes.statement: Let G be locally profinite and (ρ, V) admissible with a unitary structure. For every subrepresentation U ⊆ V the orthogonal complement U^⊥ is a subrepresentation and V = U ⊕ U^⊥ ([Cas95] Proposition 2.1.5). Consequently V is a direct sum of irreducible admissible unitarizable representations, each isomorphism class with finite multiplicity, countably many if G is second countable ([Cas95] Proposition 2.1.14; [Ber92] Proposition 41). In particular an admissible unitarizable representation of finite length is a finite direct sum of irreducibles.
hypotheses: G locally profinite; V admissible and unitarizable.
proofSteps: U^⊥ is G-stable by invariance of the form; U ∩ U^⊥ = 0 by positivity.

U + U^⊥ = V: it suffices to check on V^K for every compact open K; V^K is finite-dimensional, e_K preserves both U and U^⊥ (it is self-adjoint for the form), and the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition of V^K gives U^K + (U^⊥)^K = V^K ([Ber92] Proposition 41, proof).

Decomposition: the subrepresentation generated by V^K is finitely generated, has an irreducible quotient, which splits off by the first part; induction on dim V^K and Zorn's lemma over K give the direct sum ([Cas95] Proposition 2.1.14, proof).
acceptance: For the non-unitarizable principal series i_B(δ_B^{1/2}) of GL₂(ℚ_p), which has the trivial representation as a quotient and the Steinberg representation as a subrepresentation, the extension is non-split; so the theorem fails without a unitary structure.

sources.match: For admissible unitary V and a G-stable U, the orthogonal complement is G-stable and complementary; unitary admissible representations are direct sums of irreducible unitary admissible ones with finite multiplicities, countably many when G has a countable neighbourhood basis.

sources.locator: Ch. IV §1.2, Proposition 41 and proof, p. 86
sources.match: An admissible unitary representation is completely reducible; the proof checks W^K + (W^⊥)^K = V^K by dimension counting.

nodes.title: Normalised parabolic induction preserves unitarity
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients. Let P = MN be a parabolic subgroup and σ a unitarizable smooth representation of M. Then the normalised induction i_P^G σ (SR.2) is unitarizable: ⟪f, f'⟫ := ∫_K ⟪f(k), f'(k)⟫_σ dk for a maximal compact K with G = PK and the Haar probability measure of K, which is G-invariant because of the δ_P^{1/2} normalisation ([Ber92] Proposition 38). If σ is moreover admissible of finite length, i_P^G σ is a finite direct sum of irreducible unitarizable representations; in particular unitary principal series i_B(χ) with |χ| = 1 are semisimple.
hypotheses: G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients.
σ unitarizable; for the semisimplicity statement σ admissible of finite length.
proofSteps: Elements of i_P σ are functions f(pg) = δ_P^{1/2}(p)σ(p)f(g); the function g ↦ ⟪f(g), f'(g)⟫ transforms by δ_P on the left, i.e. is a density on P\G, whose integral over the compact P\G is G-invariant; for a special maximal compact K and a minimal parabolic Q ⊆ P the Iwasawa decomposition G = QK (ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.4) gives G = PK and writes this integral over K ([Ber92] Proposition 38, proof).
Positivity: a nonzero f is nonzero on an open subset of K.
Finite length of i_P σ (SR.3 finite-length) and admissible-unitary-semisimple give the semisimplicity.

Without normalisation the induced form fails: unnormalised Ind_B^G(1) of GL₂(ℚ_p) contains the trivial representation with a non-split quotient, so it is not unitarizable.

sources.match: Normalised induction from a parabolic subgroup takes unitary representations to unitary ones, the scalar product being the integral over G/P of the pointwise pairing, a density because of the half-density twist.
Ciubotaru–Harris call X(s) = i_{B(k)}^{G(k)}(χ_s) the (unitarily) induced spherical minimal principal series, using the normalised induction that preserves unitarity.

nodes.title: Hilbert completion of a unitarizable representation
nodes.statement: Let G be locally profinite and (ρ, V) smooth with a unitary structure. Its Hilbert completion Ĥ(V) (Mathlib's UniformSpace.Completion with the completed inner product) carries a unique strongly continuous unitary representation ρ̂ extending ρ. V ⊆ Ĥ(V)^∞, with equality Ĥ(V)^K = V^K for every compact open K when V is admissible; then Ĥ(V)^∞ = V. If V is irreducible and admissible, ρ̂ is topologically irreducible. Isomorphic irreducible unitarizable admissible representations have unitarily equivalent completions after rescaling the forms (unitary-structure-unique).
hypotheses: G locally profinite; V smooth with a unitary structure; admissibility for the statements about smooth vectors and irreducibility.
proofSteps: Each ρ(g) is isometric on V, hence extends to a linear isometry of the completion; these form a ContRepresentation, unitary because the inverses extend too.
Strong continuity: g ↦ ρ(g)v is locally constant for v ∈ V; density of V and the uniform bound ‖ρ̂(g)‖ ≤ 1 give continuity on Ĥ(V).
Smooth vectors: the projection e_K of Ĥ(V) (smooth-vectors-unitary) maps V onto V^K, so Ĥ(V)^K = e_K Ĥ(V) is the closure of V^K, which equals V^K when finite-dimensional; hence Ĥ(V)^∞ = ⋃ V^K = V.
Irreducibility: for a closed invariant W, W^∞ = ⋃_K e_K W ⊆ V is a subrepresentation, so W^∞ = 0 or V; W^∞ is dense in W (smooth-vectors-unitary), so W = 0 or Ĥ(V) ([BZ76] §4.21(c) for GL_n).
acceptance: For V finite-dimensional unitarizable, Ĥ(V) = V and ρ̂ = ρ.
For the left regular representation of a discrete group on finitely supported functions, the completion is ℓ²(G).

sources.match: An irreducible algebraic representation with an invariant positive-definite hermitian product completes to a topologically irreducible unitary representation whose algebraic part is the original space (stated for GL_n(F), not proved there).
An irreducible smooth representation is unitarizable iff it is the space of smooth vectors of an irreducible unitary representation.

one direction of the identification of the unitary dual with irreducible unitarizable smooth representations

nodes.title: Irreducible unitary representations are admissible
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients. Let (π, H) be a topologically irreducible strongly continuous unitary representation of G. Then the smooth vectors H^∞ form an admissible representation, irreducible as a smooth representation, and π is unitarily equivalent to the Hilbert completion of H^∞ (Bernstein 1974; [BZ76] §4.21(a) for GL_n). Two such representations are unitarily equivalent iff their smooth parts are isomorphic ([BZ76] §4.21(b)).
hypotheses: G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients.
proofSteps: For a compact open K, H^K is a nonzero (for small K) closed subspace on which the Hecke algebra H(G, K; ℂ) acts by bounded operators, as a *-representation, and topologically irreducibly (a closed H(G,K)-stable subspace of H^K generates a closed G-stable subspace of H whose K-fixed part it is).

By uniform admissibility (SR.3a uniform-admissibility) every simple H(G, K)-module has dimension ≤ c(G, K); this bounded-dimension property passes to the topologically irreducible *-representations of the C*-closure of H(G, K) (a polynomial-identity argument, Godement and Kaplansky as invoked in [BZ76] §4.21), so dim H^K ≤ c(G, K) < ∞.

Hence H^∞ is admissible; it is irreducible because a proper subrepresentation would have a closure that is a proper closed invariant subspace (its K-fixed parts are those of the subrepresentation); hilbert-completion identifies H with the completion of H^∞.
Equivalence: an isomorphism of smooth parts transports the unitary structure up to a scalar (unitary-structure-unique) and extends to the completions.
acceptance: For G compact the theorem says irreducible unitary representations are finite-dimensional, as in Peter–Weyl.

For a discrete group that is not virtually abelian, irreducible unitary representations need not have finite-dimensional K-fixed spaces (K = {e}); reductivity of G is used through uniform admissibility.

sources.locator: §4.21, Theorem (a)–(b) and the sentence before it, p. 43
sources.match: For G = GL_n(F), the algebraic part of a topologically irreducible unitary representation is admissible and irreducible, and unitary equivalence matches isomorphism of algebraic parts; the theorem is deduced from the bound s(G, N) on dimensions of representations of the Hecke algebra and Godement's results.

sources.locator: I. N. Bernstein, All reductive p-adic groups are tame, Funct. Anal. Appl. 8 (1974) (not read)
sources.match: The general reductive case of the admissibility of irreducible unitary representations.
The bound c(G, K) on dim V^K for irreducible smooth V, equivalently on simple H(G, K; ℂ)-modules, for any reductive G over F.

nodes.title: The unitary dual as unitarizable smooth representations
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients. The maps [π] ↦ (π^∞ = H^∞) and V ↦ [completion of V] are inverse bijections between the unitary dual Ĝ (SRU.0) and the set of isomorphism classes of irreducible unitarizable smooth representations of G. Under this bijection the positive-type coefficient of a smooth unit vector v is g ↦ ⟪v, ρ(g)v⟫ computed in V; the Fell topology (SRU.1) is described by such coefficients of smooth vectors; and the trivial, Steinberg (SR.3.4), square-integrable and unitary-induced representations define points of Ĝ.
hypotheses: G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a nonarchimedean local field F, with the conventions of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups (SR) and complex coefficients.
proofSteps: Well defined: unitary-irreducibles-admissible gives irreducible admissible π^∞, unitarizable by restriction of the inner product; hilbert-completion gives a topologically irreducible completion.
The two composites are the identity up to isomorphism (unitary-irreducibles-admissible, last clause; hilbert-completion, smooth vectors).
Coefficients of smooth vectors suffice for the Fell topology by density of smooth vectors and dist_ptCoeff_le.

Square-integrable irreducible representations are unitarizable (SR.3.3 square-integrable-tempered), in particular the Steinberg representation of a split group (SR.3.4 steinberg); unitary induction gives the tempered ones (unitary-induction).
acceptance: For G = F^× the bijection identifies Ĝ with the unitary smooth characters of F^×.
The Steinberg representation of GL₂(ℚ_p), being square-integrable modulo a unitary central character, defines a point of the unitary dual of PGL₂(ℚ_p).

sources.match: Gan–Savin work with smooth representations: an irreducible smooth representation is unitarizable iff it is the smooth part of an irreducible unitary representation, and limit points are defined through coefficients of these.
The unitary–algebraic dictionary for GL_n(F).

nodes.title: Weak convergence of distribution characters
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a p-adic field F of characteristic zero (Gan–Savin take 𝐆 split simple), complex coefficients, a fixed Haar measure dg on G. For an admissible representation π of finite length, Θ_π(f) = tr π(f), f ∈ C_c^∞(G), is its distribution character (π(f) = ∫ f(g)π(g) dg has finite rank; EndoscopicTransfer ET.4). A sequence (πₙ) of admissible finite-length representations has weakly convergent characters when Θ_{πₙ}(f) converges for every f ∈ C_c^∞(G); the limit Θ := lim Θ_{πₙ} is a linear functional on C_c^∞(G), invariant under conjugation. Gan–Savin write C_c(G) for the test space; for a p-adic group the space on which characters are defined is C_c^∞(G) of locally constant compactly supported functions, the reading used here. Characters are additive in short exact sequences, so Θ factors through the Grothendieck group of finite-length representations.
hypotheses: G = 𝐆(F) with 𝐆 connected reductive over a p-adic field F of characteristic zero (Gan–Savin take 𝐆 split simple), complex coefficients, a fixed Haar measure dg on G.
proofSteps: π(f) = e_K π(f) e_K for K with f K-bi-invariant, and π(f) acts on the finite-dimensional V^K ([Cas95] §2.3).
Additivity: for 0 → V' → V → V'' → 0 admissible, π(f) is block triangular on V^K = V'^K ⊕ V''^K (exactness of K-invariants, SR.0 invariants-exact), so traces add.
Conjugation invariance: tr π(f ∘ Ad g) = tr(π(g)⁻¹π(f)π(g)).
acceptance: Constant sequences converge weakly.
If Θ_{πₙ} → Θ and Θ_{π'ₙ} → Θ' then Θ_{πₙ ⊕ π'ₙ} → Θ + Θ'.

sources.match: A sequence of characters χ_{πₙ} is weakly converging if χ_{πₙ}(f) converges for every test function f.

sources.locator: §2.3, definition of the distribution character, p. 25
sources.match: For admissible π and f ∈ H(G) the operator π(f) has finite rank; its trace is the distribution character, depending on the Haar measure.
